name: Level Up
focus: Composing, music for games and screen

assessment.name: AT4: Level Up
assessment.type: Composed cue, process log and rationale

lessons.title: Motif: the smallest usable idea
lessons.intention: We are learning to generate musical material from a small idea.
criteria: I can write a motif and develop it using at least two devices.
steps: What a motif is and what makes one usable: short, distinctive, and able to survive being changed.
Compositional devices for generating material from a motif: repetition, sequence, inversion, augmentation, fragmentation.
Students generate four motifs in flat.io and keep the two that survive development.
lessons.enduring: A motif is built to be developed, not to be finished.

lessons.title: Leitmotif: an idea attached to something
lessons.intention: We are learning how a motif can carry meaning across a whole work.
criteria: I can transform a motif so it means something different but stays recognisable.
steps: Leitmotif as a technique: a motif attached to a character, place or idea, and changed as that thing changes.
Two contrasting screen works from the register examined for how the leitmotif is transformed.
Students attach one of their motifs to a character and write two transformations of it.
resources: Listening set from the repertoire register.
lessons.enduring: The same idea, changed, is how music tells a story over time.

lessons.title: Why game music loops and film music does not
lessons.intention: We are learning how a piece of music's purpose shapes what it is.
criteria: I can explain how the purpose of a cue changes the way it is written.
steps: The relationship between context and purpose: a film cue is written once for a fixed length; a game loop is written for an unknown one.
Two excerpts compared for how each solves its own problem.
Written response: one dot point on purpose and one on a musical feature that serves it.
lessons.enduring: Context and purpose are musical facts, not background information.

lessons.title: AT4 issued, with the blueprint
lessons.contentPoint: Conventions of styles and media combined
lessons.intention: We are learning what AT4 asks for and what it supplies.
criteria: I can explain what is given to me in this task and what I have to bring.
steps: Assessment Task 4 issued: a cue composed in flat.io, with the process log and a 250-word rationale, due Week 8.
The scaffolding handed over with it: the timing sheet with the hit points marked, the flat.io template and the motif bank. The harmonic frame is not supplied.
How conventions of different media combine, and which convention each student is writing inside.
lessons.enduring: Conventions of different styles and media can be combined to create meaning.

lessons.title: Adaptive music, layered stems and the stinger
lessons.intention: We are learning how music can change in response to what a player does.
criteria: I can write two layers that work alone and together.
steps: How game music changes with the player: layered stems added and removed, and stingers triggered by events.
One game score examined for how the layers are built so that any combination works.
Students build a two-layer loop in flat.io where either layer works alone.
lessons.enduring: Adaptive music is a form problem before it is a technology problem.

lessons.title: Building a loop that bears repeating
lessons.contentPoint: Combining styles to create new ideas
lessons.intention: We are learning to combine styles and to write music that bears repetition.
criteria: I can write an eight-bar loop that is still bearable after twenty plays.
steps: What makes a loop survive its twentieth repetition: harmony that does not resolve too hard, variation inside it, and a seam that does not click.
Styles combined to create new ideas: an orchestral gesture over an electronic pulse, and what that combination means.
Each student's loop played twenty times in a row and judged.
lessons.enduring: Looping music has to bear repetition, which is a different problem from holding attention once.

lessons.title: Two media combined
lessons.contentPoint: Conventions of styles and media combined
lessons.intention: We are learning how conventions from different media are combined.
criteria: I can name the conventions my cue borrows and say why.
steps: The game that scores like a film, and the film that scores like a game: conventions borrowed across media and what is gained.
Two works from the register compared for the conventions they mix.
Students identify which conventions their own cue will borrow.
lessons.enduring: Combining conventions deliberately is a compositional decision.

lessons.title: Context and purpose: what the music is for
lessons.intention: We are learning to examine the relationship between context and purpose.
criteria: I can explain what a cue is for and which element achieves it.
steps: The relationship between a work's context and its purpose examined in three cues written for different jobs.
What the audience is being made to feel, and which element is doing it.
Timed writing: two dot points, one on purpose and one on the element that serves it.
lessons.enduring: Music written for a job can be judged against the job.

lessons.title: Motif development: taking the bank apart
lessons.intention: We are learning to choose material we can actually develop.
criteria: I can choose a motif and show three developments of it.
steps: The supplied motif bank examined: what each motif is built from and what it will and will not do.
Each student selects or writes their motif for AT4 and develops it three ways.
The choice and the developments logged.
lessons.enduring: Choosing material well is choosing what will still be interesting in bar forty.

lessons.title: Reading a timing sheet
lessons.contentPoint: Composing for different purposes and audiences
lessons.intention: We are learning to write music to a fixed clock.
criteria: I can choose a tempo that makes my hit points land on strong beats.
steps: The timing sheet read and understood: events, times and which ones the music has to land on.
Tempo chosen so the hit points fall on musically useful beats, taught as arithmetic rather than as luck.
Each student marks their own hit points in the flat.io template.
lessons.enduring: Writing to picture is writing to somebody else's clock.

lessons.title: Scoring to picture: the first 30 seconds
lessons.contentPoint: Composing for different purposes and audiences
lessons.intention: We are learning to compose for a specific purpose and audience.
criteria: I can write 30 seconds of music that fits the scene it was written for.
steps: The opening of the cue written to the picture, in the style and for the audience the brief names.
Entry, first hit point and the first change of mood, written and played against the scene.
Draft played against picture in class.
lessons.enduring: A cue is judged against the picture, not on its own.

lessons.title: Draft checkpoint 1
lessons.intention: We are learning to annotate a draft so it communicates our intent.
criteria: I can mark my score so another player knows how to play it.
steps: First logged checkpoint. Each draft annotated with dynamics, articulation and expressive markings so a player would know what was meant.
Why an unmarked score is an incomplete message, shown by having a classmate play an unmarked part.
Feedback on process, not a preview mark.
lessons.enduring: Notation without markings is only half the message.

lessons.title: Orchestration and register
lessons.intention: We are learning how interpretation changes with instrumentation and orchestration.
criteria: I can orchestrate the same material two ways and explain the difference.
steps: Who plays the idea, and what changes when somebody else plays it: the same eight bars heard in four orchestrations.
Register as a decision: the same line an octave lower is a different statement.
Students re-orchestrate their own opening two ways and choose.
lessons.enduring: Orchestration is a decision about meaning, not only about who is available.

lessons.title: Changing the instrumentation, changing the meaning
lessons.intention: We are learning to examine how interpretation is affected by orchestration.
criteria: I can explain how a change of instrumentation changed the meaning.
steps: A professional cue examined in two versions, and what the change of forces does to the meaning.
Interpretation as something affected by orchestration rather than added to it.
Written response: one dot point on an orchestration decision and its effect.
lessons.enduring: The same notes, differently scored, say different things.

lessons.title: Markings that tell a player what you meant
lessons.intention: We are learning to annotate a score appropriately to its style.
criteria: I can mark my score so a sight-reader plays it the way I intended.
steps: Dynamics, articulation and expressive markings applied across the whole draft, appropriately to the style.
Style-specific conventions: what an orchestral part expects and what a rhythm section part expects.
Peer test: a classmate sight-reads a passage and reports what they understood.
lessons.enduring: The test of a marking is whether a stranger plays it right.

lessons.title: Composing for the audience and the purpose
lessons.contentPoint: Composing for different purposes and audiences
lessons.intention: We are learning to compose in a style and for a purpose.
criteria: I can keep my cue consistent with the style and purpose I named.
steps: The middle of the cue written, with the purpose and the audience restated before work begins.
Composing in a style for a stated purpose, and checking the writing against both.
Draft played against picture and adjusted.
lessons.enduring: A brief is a constraint that makes the decisions easier, not harder.

lessons.title: Draft checkpoint 2
lessons.intention: We are learning to review a full draft against the brief.
criteria: I can review my whole cue and list what still has to change.
steps: Second logged checkpoint. Full draft reviewed for markings, playability and whether the hit points still land.
Reflection recorded in the log on what changed between checkpoints one and two.
Rationale drafting begins next week, so the log is read now with that in view.
lessons.enduring: A checkpoint is for finding the gap, not for confirming progress.

lessons.title: Texture and layering
lessons.intention: We are learning to write layers that work in more than one combination.
criteria: I can build layers that still work when one is removed.
steps: Layers built so they can be turned on and off, for the game brief, or so the texture thins and thickens with the scene, for the film brief.
How changes in instrumentation affect the interpretation of the same layer in a different combination.
Stems exported and played in combinations.
lessons.enduring: Writing in layers is writing several versions of the same music at once.

lessons.title: The 250-word rationale
lessons.intention: We are learning to explain compositional decisions in writing.
criteria: I can write about a decision I made and connect it to what the cue is for.
steps: What the rationale has to do: name the decisions, use the terminology, and connect each decision to the brief.
Deliberately half of Year 10 AT1's 500 words, so the rationale is a step rather than a cliff.
A model rationale read and marked against the criteria, then a weak one.
lessons.enduring: Evaluating your own work in writing is how the decisions become deliberate.

lessons.title: Rationale drafted and workshopped
lessons.intention: We are learning to use feedback to refine our own writing and work.
criteria: I can revise my rationale so every claim points at something in the music.
steps: First draft of the rationale written from the process log rather than from memory.
Peer feedback on whether each claim is supported by something audible in the cue.
Feedback used to refine, and the refinement logged.
lessons.enduring: A claim that cannot be pointed at in the music is not a claim.

lessons.title: Sound sources, samples and intellectual property
lessons.intention: We are learning the protocols that apply to the material we compose with.
criteria: I can say where every sound in my project came from and whether I may use it.
steps: Where the sounds came from: samples, libraries, licences and what may be used in submitted work.
Protocols for information, identity and intellectual property when composing and when sharing.
Each student audits their own project for anything that needs attribution.
lessons.enduring: Knowing what you may use is part of composing with technology.

lessons.title: Final revision against the rationale
lessons.intention: We are learning to evaluate our own success in communicating intent.
criteria: I can make the cue and the rationale agree with each other.
steps: The cue revised so that what the rationale claims is actually true of the music.
Where the two disagree, one of them changes, and the log records which and why.
Final playback against picture.
lessons.enduring: The rationale and the piece are one submission, not two.

lessons.title: AT4 due
lessons.intention: We are learning to submit composed work complete and correctly attributed.
criteria: I can submit all three parts of the task with correct attribution.
steps: Assessment Task 4 submitted: the cue in flat.io, the process log and the 250-word rationale.
Submission protocols: attribution, file naming and what is included.
Students state one thing they would do differently with another fortnight.
lessons.enduring: The submission is the cue, the log and the rationale together.

lessons.title: Sharing work: what may be posted
lessons.intention: We are learning the protocols that apply when compositions are shared.
criteria: I can decide what from my project may be shared and justify it.
steps: What may and may not be shared publicly from this project, and why the answer differs from the answer for a live cover.
Identity and information online, applied to a portfolio a student might actually build.
Sharing decisions recorded for the showcase next week.
lessons.enduring: Sharing decisions are made before the work is posted, not afterwards.

lessons.title: Showcase: cues played to the class
lessons.contentPoint: Analysing elements in own and others' compositions
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse the elements of music in our own compositions and in others'.
criteria: I can present my cue and discuss how I used the elements in it.
steps: Cues played against their scenes to the class, with the composer introducing the brief in one sentence.
The elements analysed as each is heard, with the composer answering.
Recorded for the evidence file.
lessons.enduring: Presenting the work is where the analysis becomes public.

lessons.title: Evaluating the elements in our cues
lessons.contentPoint: Analysing elements in own and others' compositions
lessons.intention: We are learning to discuss the use of the elements in our own and others' compositions.
criteria: I can analyse a classmate's cue and my own using precise terminology.
steps: Three cues analysed in depth by the class, one film and two game, with the composers present.
Each student then writes the same analysis of their own work.
Vocabulary from the term used precisely and corrected where it is not.
lessons.enduring: Analysing your own work is the same skill as analysing anyone else's.

lessons.title: Listening beyond the unit
lessons.intention: We are learning to evaluate musical features and the communication of ideas.
criteria: I can evaluate an unfamiliar work and support the judgement.
steps: A live or recorded work heard and evaluated in full, outside the unit's repertoire, for how it communicates its ideas.
The year's listening skills applied to something nobody prepared for.
Written response in the AT3 format, unmarked.
lessons.enduring: Listening skill is only useful if it works on music nobody chose for you.

lessons.title: What Year 10 asks for next
lessons.intention: We are learning where this year's work leads next.
criteria: I can name what Year 10 will expect and where my work already meets it.
steps: Year 10 AT1 previewed: a minute of programme music in flat.io with a 500-word rationale, and how AT4 was the rung below it.
The Year 10 units named, and what each will assume this class already has.
Students evaluate one of their own works against the Year 10 criteria for interest.
resources: AT4 and Year 10 AT1 criteria side by side.
lessons.enduring: The next rung is visible from this one, which is what makes it a rung.

lessons.title: Performance check-in
lessons.intention: We are learning to evaluate our own technique and target the next step.
criteria: I can name one technical target for next year and say why.
steps: Each student plays something, and evaluates their own technique against where they were in Term 1.
A technical target set for Year 10, written down and kept.
Ensemble plays one piece from each term of the year.
lessons.enduring: Evaluating technique is what turns practice into progress.

lessons.title: The year closed
lessons.intention: We are learning to evaluate a year's work as a whole.
criteria: I can show, with evidence from my log, what changed in my musicianship.
steps: The process log read end to end, from the Term 1 songwriting block to the AT4 rationale.
Each student writes one page on what changed in their musicianship this year, with evidence from the log.
Reports are written in this window; evidence gathered here still counts toward the on-balance judgement.
lessons.enduring: A log kept all year is worth reading all at once.
